blindSummary:
This state/province carries the country's most heavily documented sub-national enforcement pattern against trans people: the national human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to a UN human-rights treaty body documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by the state/provincial police - or by third parties under police cover - against trans and travesti people during operations in the state/province's administrative capital, a major coastal city and a third municipality, carried out under 'preventive policing' frameworks. Academic legal analysis (a human-rights NGO's shadow report to a UN women's-discrimination treaty body; a national-university study; a criminal-law journal) confirms that after the 2012 national gender-identity law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution (devolved to state/provincial justice in 2005) and street-offence law as the operative instrument for indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity - a patterned, state-implicated escalation with impunity.

No other state/province has a comparable volume of multi-source, patterned enforcement documentation reaching the UN treaty-body system. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework (drug-law devolution plus an anti-narcotics security policy) that measurably increased police persecution of trans women. Protective institutions coexist - the state/province's public-defender office maintains a 2024 registry-rectification guide and documents discrimination caseloads - but these are resident-facing and do not offset the visitor-facing exposure to arbitrary detention during any police stop.

Compared with the adjacent federal capital district, this state/province lacks that district's contravention-court judicial-oversight structure and anti-discrimination apparatus; its police-judge model under the provincial contravention code gives less post-detention review. Compared with the silent majority of states/provinces, the difference is one of documented enforcement pattern rather than statutory hostility - no state/provincial law criminalises gender identity here, but enforcement practice does the work.
blindSourceSummaries: Provincial public-defender office submission (2016) to a UN human-rights treaty body: documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by state/provincial police - or by third parties under police cover - against trans and travesti people during operations in three municipalities (the administrative capital, a coastal city and an outlying one) under 'preventive policing' frameworks; the core multi-city, state-implicated pattern behind this state/province's record.

Human-rights NGO shadow report to a UN women's-discrimination treaty body (2017): situates the state/provincial findings in the national picture - indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity through drug and street-offence prosecution after the 2012 national gender-identity law, with police-abuse documentation reaching the treaty-body system.

National-university legal study: analysis of how drug-law prosecution - devolved to state/provincial justice here in 2005 - plus a provincial anti-narcotics security policy measurably increased police persecution, violence and criminalisation of trans women; the drug law as the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation.

Criminal-law journal article (2022): on the provincial contravention/street-offence code as a tool of selective policing of travesti and trans people, and the state/province's police-judge detention model - the enforcement-practice counterpart to the formally decriminalised situation.

Provincial public-defender office's 2024 official guide to registry rectification under the national gender-identity law, with discrimination-caseload documentation - evidence of a functioning protective bureaucracy coexisting with the policing problem (resident-facing).
